162.title: Worth a third of the Qur'an
162.word: Worth a third of the Qur'an
162.hook: the Prophet ﷺ said this short surah equals a third of the Qur'an (Bukhari)
162.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite al-Ikhlas often, in the prayers, at night and before sleep, and some recite it three times in memory of the hadith that it equals a third of the Qur'an.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ahad, one with no second, from Surah al-Ikhlas. Your line was he is one. When the day pulled you in five directions, did one thing get to be the center? Day one hundred sixty-two.

Some things weigh more than their size. A wedding ring. A two-line text that says we need to talk. A child's drawing on the fridge. Yesterday we read a surah of four lines, fifteen words in Arabic. Today, a strange claim about it, made by the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself, and recorded in the most trusted collection of hadith. Four lines, he said, weigh as much as a third of the whole Qur'an. Six thousand verses, and these fifteen words are a third? Today: worth a third of the Qur'an.
screen: `SMALL THINGS THAT WEIGH A LOT.` → `FIFTEEN WORDS.` → `A THIRD OF THE WHOLE BOOK?`

segments.voice: The hadith is in Sahih al-Bukhari. A companion heard a man reciting qul huwa Allahu ahad at night, over and over, nothing else. In the morning he told the Prophet, a little as if the man were cutting corners. The Prophet answered: by the One in whose hand my soul is, it equals a third of the Qur'an. Another report in Bukhari has him asking his companions, can any of you recite a third of the Qur'an in a night? They said, who could manage that? And he told them: this surah is a third. So what does it mean? Scholars have offered a well-known answer. The Qur'an, they say, speaks of three great things: who Allah is; what He commands, the law; and what happens, the stories and the promise of what's coming. Al-Ikhlas is the first of those, pure and whole. It's all about who God is. Scholars add a caution: it equals a third in reward and meaning, not as a substitute. Reciting it three times doesn't mean you've read the whole book. There's one more story. A man leading his companions in prayer ended every recitation with this surah. They complained to the Prophet. He said: ask him why. The man said: because it describes the Most Merciful, and I love to recite it. And the Prophet said: tell him that Allah loves him. Short, and heavy. The weight isn't in the length. It's in what the words hold, and in the love of the one reciting them.
screen: `OVER AND OVER, ALL NIGHT.` · `IT EQUALS A THIRD OF THE QUR'AN.` · `WHO GOD IS, WHAT GOD ASKS, WHAT HAPPENS.` · `TELL HIM ALLAH LOVES HIM.` · then, large: `SHORT, AND HEAVY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: slowly. If you pray, you can recite al-Ikhlas slowly in one of today's prayers, or right now, one line per breath, letting each line land before the next. If you don't, pick one short line you love from anywhere, and say it as slowly as you've ever said anything. Notice how much room there is inside something small when you don't rush it. The bell holds the time.
Worth a third of the Qur'an. What the Prophet said of Surah al-Ikhlas: four lines about who Allah is, heavy with meaning and reward. Today's word.
screen: `WORTH A THIRD OF THE QUR'AN — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: short, and heavy. Today, say one short thing that matters, and say it slowly: thank you, I'm sorry, I love you. Let it weigh what it weighs. Day one hundred sixty-two.

163.title: Al-Masad: the palm-fiber rope
163.hook: a warning about Abu Lahab, the Prophet's own uncle and enemy (Surah 111)
163.howItsDone: Surah al-Masad, also called al-Lahab, is recited in the prayers like other short surahs; Muslims learn its story, the Prophet's call from Safa and his uncle's reply, as part of the life of the Prophet.

segments.voice: Yesterday: al-Ikhlas, worth a third of the Qur'an. Your line was short, and heavy. Did you say one short thing slowly, and did it weigh more than usual? Day one hundred sixty-three.

Every family has someone. The uncle who turns every holiday dinner into an argument. The cousin who takes your news and makes it about himself. Most of the time it's small. For the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ it was not small. His uncle, his father's own brother, became one of his fiercest public enemies. And the Qur'an names him. Only one of the Prophet's opponents in Mecca is named in the Qur'an, and it's this man, family. Today: Al-Masad, the palm-fiber rope.
screen: `EVERY FAMILY HAS SOMEONE.` → `HIS OWN UNCLE.` → `THE ONLY ENEMY NAMED.`

segments.voice: The story is in Sahih al-Bukhari. When the Prophet was told to warn his own clan, he climbed the hill of Safa in Mecca and called out to the families of Quraysh, one by one, until they gathered. He asked: if I told you an army was behind this hill, would you believe me? They said: we've never known you to lie. Then, he said, I am a warner to you before a severe punishment. And his uncle, Abu Lahab, answered: may you perish! Is this what you gathered us for? The surah answers him, with his own word. Pickthall translates the first line: The power of Abu Lahab will perish, and he will perish. Abu Lahab wasn't his real name. It means father of flame, a nickname, some say for his glowing, ruddy face. The surah says his wealth and his gains won't help him. It names his wife too, who, commentators say, scattered thorns in the Prophet's path: she'll carry firewood, with a rope of palm fiber, masad, around her neck. The surah is named for that rope. Here's what scholars point out. The Prophet's family didn't protect Abu Lahab. Being the Prophet's uncle, the closest possible tie, was not a guarantee of anything. And the reverse is true in the same story: another uncle, Abu Talib, protected the Prophet for years. Two brothers, the same nephew, two different choices. Kin is not a guarantee. Not of harm, not of goodness. What counts, in the Qur'an's telling, is what each person does.
screen: `A CALL FROM THE HILL OF SAFA.` · `MAY YOU PERISH — HIS UNCLE'S ANSWER.` · `A ROPE OF PALM FIBER.` · `TWO UNCLES, TWO CHOICES.` · then, large: `KIN IS NOT A GUARANTEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and think of your family, the one you were born into or the one you've made. Notice one person whose closeness to you has been a gift, and one relationship where being related hasn't made things good. Don't judge either one. Just hold both as true. Then turn it around, gently: being part of your family isn't a guarantee for you either. What would you want your own choices to add? The bell holds the time.
Al-Masad. The palm-fiber rope, the name of Surah one hundred eleven, about the Prophet's uncle Abu Lahab. Today's word.
Your line: kin is not a guarantee. Today, notice when you assume someone is good, or bad, because of who they belong to. Look at what they do instead. Day one hundred sixty-three.

164.title: An-Nasr: the help
164.hook: when help comes and people enter in crowds, praise and ask forgiveness (Surah 110)
164.howItsDone: Many Muslims say astaghfirullah and subhan Allah after a success, following this surah; the Prophet's words in bowing and prostration after it was revealed are still said by many in their prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Masad, and the uncle whose kinship didn't protect him. Your line was kin is not a guarantee. Did you catch yourself judging someone by who they belong to? Day one hundred sixty-four.

Think about the last time you won something. A game, an argument, a promotion, a parking spot. What did you do with the first ten seconds? A fist in the air, maybe. A text to someone who doubted you. It's the most natural thing in the world. Yesterday's surah was about the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ at the start, rejected by his own family on a hill in Mecca. Today's is about the end, when everything he'd hoped for came true. And what it tells him to do with the first ten seconds is not what you'd expect. Today: An-Nasr, the help.
screen: `THE FIRST TEN SECONDS OF WINNING.` → `FROM REJECTION TO VICTORY.` → `NOT WHAT YOU'D EXPECT.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred ten, in Pickthall's translation: When Allah's succour and the triumph cometh And thou seest mankind entering the religion of Allah in troops, Then hymn the praises of thy Lord, and seek forgiveness of Him. Lo! He is ever ready to show mercy. Nasr means help, the kind that turns a struggle. Most commentators connect the surah with the opening of Mecca, around the year six hundred thirty, when the city that had driven the Prophet out opened to him, and people came to Islam in whole tribes at a time. Now look at the instruction. Not celebrate. Not remind them who was right. Praise your Lord, and ask forgiveness. Why forgiveness, at the moment of victory? Scholars give two answers. First, success is exactly when a person is most likely to forget where it came from, so you ask forgiveness for whatever pride slipped in. Second, a deeper reading. Bukhari records that Umar asked the senior companions what the surah meant, and most said it was a command to praise at victory. Then he asked the young Ibn Abbas, who said: it's the sign that the Prophet's time is near. His work is finished. Umar said: I know nothing of it except what you know. The Prophet died about two years after the opening of Mecca. Aisha reports that after this surah came, he would often say in his bowing and prostration: glory be to You, our Lord, and praise; O Allah, forgive me. And the sirah describes him entering Mecca with his head bowed so low it nearly touched his saddle. Win humbly.
screen: `NASR — THE HELP THAT TURNS IT.` · `THE OPENING OF MECCA.` · `PRAISE, AND ASK FORGIVENESS.` · `THE SIGN THAT HIS TIME WAS NEAR.` · then, large: `WIN HUMBLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and bring back a recent success, even a small one. Something that went right, that you're a little proud of. Feel it. Now notice who and what helped: people, timing, things you didn't control. If you pray, you can say astaghfirullah, I seek Allah's forgiveness, for any pride that slipped in. If you don't, simply let a little of the credit go back to where it came from. The bell holds the time.
An-Nasr. The help, the name of Surah one hundred ten: when help and victory come, praise your Lord and ask forgiveness. Today's word.
Your line: win humbly. The next time something goes your way today, spend the first ten seconds on thanks, not on proving anyone wrong. Day one hundred sixty-four.

165.title: Al-Kafirun: to you your way
165.hook: you have your way and I have mine (109:6)
165.carry: to you yours, to me mine
165.howItsDone: Many Muslims recite al-Kafirun and al-Ikhlas in the two sunnah units of prayer before the dawn prayer, as the Prophet did, and some recite al-Kafirun before sleep.

segments.voice: Yesterday: An-Nasr, praise and forgiveness at the moment of victory. Your line was win humbly. When something went your way, where did the first ten seconds go? Day one hundred sixty-five.

You know the offer. Let's split the difference. You come to my thing this week, I'll come to yours next week. In most of life, that's how peace gets made: a little give on both sides. The leaders of Mecca, the commentators say, made the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ an offer like that. We'll worship your God for a year, and you worship our gods for a year. Everybody wins. Everybody calms down. The answer was a surah of six lines, and its last line is one of the most quoted in the Qur'an. Today: Al-Kafirun, to you your way.
screen: `LET'S SPLIT THE DIFFERENCE.` → `A YEAR FOR YOURS, A YEAR FOR OURS.` → `SIX LINES IN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The surah opens: say, O disbelievers. Kafirun means those who cover over, who reject; here, the Meccan leaders who made the offer. Then it turns in a slow circle. I don't worship what you worship. And you don't worship what I worship. And I won't worship what you worship. And you won't worship what I worship. The repetition is the point. It closes the negotiation from every side: not now, not later, not in turns. And then the last line, in Pickthall's translation: Unto you your religion, and unto me my religion. Two things are true about that line, and scholars hold both. First, it draws a clear boundary in worship. The Prophet would not mix his worship with theirs, even for peace. Most classical scholars read the surah this way: a declaration that worship isn't something you trade. Second, the boundary is drawn without a threat. It doesn't say: and so we will make you. It says: yours is yours, mine is mine. Many Muslims, especially today, read that line alongside another verse, in Surah al-Baqarah, that there is no compulsion in religion, as a basis for living honestly beside people who believe differently. Scholars have discussed how far that second reading goes; it's a live conversation. The Prophet recited this surah often. A hadith in Muslim says he recited it, with al-Ikhlas, in the two short prayers before the dawn prayer. One surah says who God is. The other says clearly where you stand, and leaves others their own place.
screen: `THE OFFER: TAKE TURNS WORSHIPPING.` · `NOT NOW, NOT LATER, NOT IN TURNS.` · `A BOUNDARY WITHOUT A THREAT.` · `WITH AL-IKHLAS, BEFORE DAWN.` · then, large: `TO YOU YOURS, TO ME MINE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Bring to mind one disagreement you're carrying, with someone whose view you really don't share, about faith, politics, how to live. Notice the urge to win it, or to blur it so it goes away. Try a third thing. Let it stand. Say to yourself: this is theirs, and this is mine. Feel what it's like to hold your ground and still wish them peace. The bell holds the time.
Al-Kafirun. The disbelievers, the name of Surah one hundred nine, which ends: to you your religion, and to me mine. Today's word.

Your line: to you yours, to me mine. When a disagreement comes up today, don't trade away what matters to you, and don't try to take away what matters to them. Let it stand, peacefully. Day one hundred sixty-five.

166.title: Al-Kawthar: abundance
166.hook: We have given you abundance, so pray and sacrifice (Surah 108)
166.howItsDone: Al-Kawthar is often among the first surahs children memorize and is recited in the prayers; the hadith of the river of al-Kawthar is widely taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Kafirun, a boundary drawn without a threat. Your line was to you yours, to me mine. Did you let a disagreement stand, peacefully? Day one hundred sixty-six.
screen: `AL-KAFIRUN — TO YOU YOURS, TO ME MINE.`

segments.voice: People can be cruel about grief. In Mecca, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ lost his sons in childhood, each one. And some of his enemies, the commentators say, turned that loss into an insult. They called him abtar: cut off, a tree with no branches, a man whose name would die with him. Imagine hearing that about your children, in the street. The answer came in the shortest surah in the whole Qur'an. Three lines. Ten words in Arabic. And it doesn't start with the insult. It starts with a gift. Today: Al-Kawthar, abundance.
screen: `A LOSS TURNED INTO AN INSULT.` → `ABTAR — CUT OFF.` → `THE SHORTEST SURAH.`

segments.voice: Surah one hundred eight begins, in Pickthall's translation: Lo! We have given thee Abundance; So pray unto thy Lord, and sacrifice. Kawthar comes from the root k-th-r, much, many. It's an intensive form: not just a lot, but overflowing, more than enough. Commentators give it two meanings, and hold both. The first is every good thing given to the Prophet: the revelation, his followers, his name. The second is specific. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says the Prophet dozed off among his companions, then lifted his head smiling. They asked why. He said a surah had just come to him, and recited this one. Then he asked: do you know what al-Kawthar is? It's a river my Lord has promised me in Paradise, with abundant good. The third line turns to the insult. Lo! it is thy insulter, and not thou, who is without posterity. The word is the same one they used: abtar. History is the commentary. The Prophet's name is spoken today by well over a billion people, and his family line, through his daughter Fatima, is honored across the Muslim world. The men who mocked him are remembered mostly because this surah answered them. Notice what the gift asks for in return. Not a speech, not revenge. So pray, and sacrifice: turn toward your Lord, and give something away. That's the pattern the surah teaches. When you're told you have nothing, count what you've actually been given. Given plenty.
screen: `KAWTHAR — OVERFLOWING, MORE THAN ENOUGH.` · `A RIVER PROMISED IN PARADISE.` · `THE INSULTER IS THE ONE CUT OFF.` · `SO PRAY, AND GIVE.` · then, large: `GIVEN PLENTY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count your abundance. Sit, and start with things that are easy to miss. Breath. Your hands. Water that comes out of a tap. Then people: one who loves you, one who taught you something. Then small good things from this week. Count them slowly, on your fingers if you like. When you run out of fingers, keep going. If you pray, you can end with alhamdulillah. The bell holds the time.
Al-Kawthar. Abundance, overflowing good, and a river promised to the Prophet; the name of the shortest surah. Today's word.

Your line: given plenty. When you feel like you're running short today, of time, money, patience, stop and name three things you were given anyway. Then give one small thing away. Day one hundred sixty-six.

167.title: Al-Ma'un: small kindnesses
167.hook: woe to those who pray for show and refuse small kindnesses (Surah 107)
167.carry: the small kindness is the test
167.howItsDone: Muslims recite al-Ma'un in the prayers and often cite it as a reminder that prayer and everyday kindness belong together: lending household things, feeding the hungry, caring for orphans.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Kawthar, abundance, given to a man his enemies called cut off. Your line was given plenty. Did you count what you'd been given, and give one small thing away? Day one hundred sixty-seven.

Your neighbor knocks. Can I borrow your ladder? Or a cup of sugar, or a phone charger, or jumper cables on a cold morning. It's nothing. It costs you almost nothing. And yet everyone knows the feeling of hesitating, or of the neighbor who always says no, just because they can. Today's surah is about exactly that. It's seven short lines, and it puts the refused cup of sugar right next to prayer, as if they belonged in the same sentence. Today: Al-Ma'un, small kindnesses.
screen: `CAN I BORROW YOUR LADDER?` → `IT COSTS ALMOST NOTHING.` → `PRAYER AND THE CUP OF SUGAR.`

segments.voice: The surah opens with a question: have you seen the one who denies the Judgment? And then, instead of describing what he believes, it describes what he does. He pushes the orphan away. He doesn't encourage feeding the poor. That's the surah's first surprise: denying the faith shows up as how you treat the vulnerable. Then it turns, and this is the second surprise, to people who pray. In Pickthall's translation: Ah, woe unto worshippers Who are heedless of their prayer; Who would be seen at worship Yet refuse small kindnesses! Ma'un is the last word of the surah. It means the small things of everyday help. The companion Ibn Mas'ud explained it this way: in the Prophet's time, they understood it as lending the bucket, the cooking pot, the axe. Household things. The kind you'd lend a neighbor without thinking. So the surah draws a line from the prayer mat to the front door. Scholars note that the warning isn't for missing a prayer here or there; it's for prayer that's heedless, done for show, prayer that doesn't reach the hands. Someone can stand in a row of worshippers, and still refuse to lend a pot. The surah calls that a contradiction. The test of the big thing, the prayer, turns out to be the small thing, the pot. Not the grand gesture or the big donation. The ladder. The charger. The cup of sugar, handed over without a sigh. The small kindness is the test.
screen: `DENIAL SHOWS IN HOW YOU TREAT THE WEAK.` · `WOE TO THE HEEDLESS WORSHIPPER.` · `MA'UN — THE BUCKET, THE POT, THE AXE.` · `FROM THE PRAYER MAT TO THE FRONT DOOR.` · then, large: `THE SMALL KINDNESS IS THE TEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and walk through your home in your mind. The kitchen, the closet, the drawer of cables. Notice the small things you own that someone near you might need: a tool, a book, an umbrella, a pan. Pick one. Picture the person who could use it: a neighbor, a coworker, a friend. Then decide: today or this week, you'll offer to lend it, before they have to ask. The bell holds the time.
Al-Ma'un. Small kindnesses, everyday help like lending a bucket or a pot; the last word and name of Surah one hundred seven. Today's word.
Your line: the small kindness is the test. Today, say yes quickly to one small request, and lend one small thing without a sigh. Day one hundred sixty-seven.

168.title: Quraysh: fed and safe
168.hook: let them worship the Lord of this House who fed them and made them safe (Surah 106)
168.howItsDone: Surah Quraysh is recited in the prayers like other short surahs, and many Muslims recall it when giving thanks for food and safety.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Al-Ma'un, the bucket and the pot. Your line was the small kindness is the test. Did you lend something small, or say yes quickly to a small request? Day one hundred sixty-eight.
screen: `AL-MA'UN — THE SMALL KINDNESS IS THE TEST.`

segments.voice: Two questions most people never ask when they wake up. Is there food today? Am I safe today? If you've never had to ask them, that's the point. They're so answered you forget they're questions. For most of human history, and for many people right now, they're the first two thoughts of the morning. Today's surah is named for a tribe, the Prophet's own tribe, and it reminds them of exactly those two things. Four lines, and a list of just two gifts. Today: Quraysh, fed and safe.
screen: `IS THERE FOOD TODAY?` → `AM I SAFE TODAY?` → `TWO GIFTS, EASY TO FORGET.`

segments.voice: Quraysh was the tribe that ran Mecca, the Prophet Muhammad's own people. Mecca sits in a dry valley where almost nothing grows. What it had was the Ka'bah, the House, and trade. Commentators explain that Quraysh sent two great caravans a year: in winter south to Yemen, in summer north to Syria. The surah's first word, ilaf, means the custom, the security of those journeys. Other tribes let the caravans pass, the commentators say, because Quraysh were the keepers of the House. So a desert town had grain, cloth and peace. Then the surah turns, in Pickthall's words: So let them worship the Lord of this House, Who hath fed them against hunger and hath made them safe from fear. Notice the logic. It doesn't threaten. It reminds. You're eating. You're safe. Where do you think that came from? Scholars often read this surah together with the one before it in the book, about the elephant, which we'll hear tomorrow. And that closes another week of short surahs. A surah worth a third of the Qur'an. An uncle whose kinship didn't save him. Winning humbly. A boundary without a threat. Abundance for a grieving man. The bucket and the pot. And now: bread and safety. All of them short. All of them, in their way, about noticing what's actually in front of you.
screen: `THE PROPHET'S OWN TRIBE.` · `TWO CARAVANS: WINTER AND SUMMER.` · `FED AGAINST HUNGER, SAFE FROM FEAR.` · `A REMINDER, NOT A THREAT.` · then, large: `FED AND SAFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and think about your last meal. Trace it back: who cooked it, who sold it, who drove it, who grew it. Then think about the place you're sitting. Is the door locked? Is the street quiet? Who keeps it that way? Let the two words rest on your breath: fed, on the in-breath; safe, on the out-breath. If you pray, you can thank Allah for both, in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Quraysh. The Prophet's tribe, the keepers of the House in Mecca, and the name of Surah one hundred six. Today's word.
Your line: fed and safe. Before you eat today, pause for one breath and notice both: there's food, and nothing is chasing you. Day one hundred sixty-eight.
